questions.q: Why does this lesson describe an unenforced policy as 'functionally a suggestion'?
options: Without enforcement, the policy competes with whatever's more convenient in the moment, and convenience usually wins
Because unenforced policies are automatically deleted from the system
Because only technical controls count as real policy at all
Because policies without enforcement are illegal in every jurisdiction
questions.explain: Enforcement is what closes the gap between a written rule and actual behavior — without it, the rule is just a statement of intent.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of organizational (not technical) enforcement?
options: Tying a manager or owner's accountability to whether their domain follows the policy
An automated role-based access control rule blocking unauthorized access
A real-time monitoring dashboard flagging violations instantly
An immutable audit log of every access attempt
questions.explain: Manager/owner accountability, training and acknowledgment, audits, and escalation paths are procedural/organizational; RBAC, monitoring, and audit trails are technical.

options: Writing governance rules as executable logic embedded directly into data pipelines
Converting every written policy into a PDF document
A policy that only applies to software engineers
A rule that has no connection to any actual data system
questions.explain: Policy-as-code turns a rule into something the system itself checks automatically, rather than something that depends on someone remembering to check it.

questions.q: Why does an audit trail matter even when enforcement is working perfectly?
options: It provides a verifiable, tamper-proof record useful for regulatory compliance and investigating issues, not just for catching failures
It has no value at all unless a violation has already occurred
It replaces the need for any other enforcement mechanism
It is only useful to executive sponsors, never to stewards
questions.explain: Audit trails support compliance proof and investigation even in a well-functioning system — their value isn't limited to catching failures after they happen.

questions.q: What does automated classification typically do, as a technical enforcement mechanism?
options: Tags sensitive data so a policy's rule has something concrete to actually apply to
Writes the company's governance policy documents automatically
Replaces the need for a data owner entirely
Only applies to paper-based records, never digital systems
questions.explain: Classification identifies which fields a rule like 'confidential customer data' actually applies to, making enforcement possible in the first place.
